text: Microsoft Defender XDR — renamed from Microsoft 365 Defender in 2023 — is Microsoft's cross-domain detection and response platform. It doesn't replace the individual Defender products; it sits on top of them, pulling their signal into one unified portal at security.microsoft.com, so an analyst stops jumping between separate consoles for each product.

Four workloads feed it. Defender for Endpoint watches devices — the EDR platform covered earlier in this path. Defender for Office 365 watches email and collaboration tools. Defender for Identity watches on-prem Active Directory domain controllers. Defender for Cloud Apps watches SaaS usage and cloud access patterns. Each can still raise its own alerts on its own.

Here's why that matters. A phishing email with a credential-harvesting link is Defender for Office 365's territory. The stolen credentials used to sign in to a SaaS app from an unusual location — that's Defender for Cloud Apps. A Pass-the-Hash attempt against a domain controller from there — Defender for Identity. A malicious payload dropped on the laptop — Defender for Endpoint. Four products, one attack.

Without unification, that's four separate alerts in four separate consoles, each looking like an unrelated, low-priority event on its own. Defender XDR correlates them into one incident with a single timeline spanning email, identity, cloud app, and endpoint, because they're evidence of one attack story, not four disconnected ones.

Worth being precise about the name: Microsoft Defender XDR is the current name, Microsoft 365 Defender is the old one, and the portal is security.microsoft.com either way. The four feeding products — Endpoint, Office 365, Identity, Cloud Apps — are the same four regardless of which name you hear a colleague or a job posting use.

Defender XDR's unified incident view isn't a replacement for Microsoft Sentinel — next lesson covers the real connector that lets Sentinel ingest Defender XDR's incidents and their raw event tables, correlating Microsoft's own cross-product story with non-Microsoft data sources inside Sentinel too, which is exactly where this chapter is headed.
